intro.heading: They know the answers. Do they do it safely?
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A new carer joined three weeks ago and has worked through the induction course on her phone between shifts. Her scores are good. Her manager is pleased and busy, and the certificate is the last thing on the induction list. But a score tells you what someone knows, not how they help a resident stand from an armchair. The senior carer has seen her once, in passing, and nothing was written down. Nobody has decided who will watch her properly. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: A new carer is added as a new starter and given her induction.
She works through the course on her phone between shifts.
Good scores. The manager is pleased.
The certificate is the last item on the induction list.
A senior carer saw her help a resident once, in passing. Nothing was noted.
Nobody has agreed who will observe her, or when.
A score and a certificate. No note of anyone watching her work.
“How do you know she is competent?” A quiz result is not an observation.

trail_close: The course was never the problem. The gap is between a good score and a recorded observation. Here is how CareStream closes it, without replacing your own judgement.

why.heading: A score shows knowledge. Competence is seen on the floor.
why.sub: Skills for Care describes assessment as covering both what a worker knows and what they do.

cards.title: Quizzes test knowing, not doing
cards.body: A carer can answer every question on safe moving and still be hesitant, rushed or unsure with a real resident in front of them.

cards.title: A passing glance is not an observation
cards.body: If nobody writes down who watched, what they saw and when, the sign off exists only in memory, and memory fades by the next inspection.

cards.title: Busy managers let it slip
cards.body: Observation needs a diary slot and a senior colleague. Without a prompt, the certificate gets filed as done and the practical never happens.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.a: It is a CPD certified course that covers the 16 standards, and it is free on every plan. It is not the regulated qualification, and a CareStream certificate shows completion, not competence. Your own observation, and your own judgement, still decide whether a carer is signed off.

items.q: What stops a certificate being issued on a quiz score alone?
items.a: The certificate is held as pending practical until a manager records an observed practical assessment with a note. For CPD courses it also waits for the short course feedback. Then it shows the sign off name and date.
You decide. Many services use a senior carer or a manager who knows the standards. CareStream does not choose or train your assessor, it records the observation you carry out.

items.q: Does the induction flow include a sign off step?
items.a: No. Induction steps are either read a policy, finished by Mark as read, or answer a question. A wrong answer must be retried and creates a Follow-up item. The observed practical is recorded separately on the course, not as a step inside the flow.

items.q: What happens when a new carer gets a question wrong?
items.a: It goes into their Follow-up tab and they get an email, at most once a day. They choose Learn & retry, a short lesson then a fresh question, or Just retry. They can retry as often as they need.

items.q: How do I know a new starter has not been forgotten?
items.a: New starters are enrolled automatically in induction flows matching their job role. You see an induction progress matrix and an overdue flag, and the staff record flags induction not started after 7 days or more.

items.q: Does it alert me on every wrong answer?
items.a: No. You see the picture in the Knowledge gaps view and the Monday digest. Nothing messages you each time someone slips.

items.q: Can I try it, and what does it cost?
items.a: You can create a free account, and the paid plans have a 14 day free trial. The course is free on every plan. See the pricing page for plan details, or register to start.

limits.heading: A course and a record, not an assessor

cards.title: It does not do the observing
cards.body: A person must watch the carer work and judge it. CareStream records that observation, with your note, and holds the certificate until it is done.

cards.title: It is not a regulated qualification
cards.body: The certificate evidences completion of a CPD certified course. It does not replace your workbook, your assessor or your own judgement.

cards.title: Adhoc follow up and translation are paid features
cards.body: The course is free on every plan. Adhoc training and translation need a paid plan, and the induction flows do not include a manager signature step.

faqs.heading: The induction course and observation, answered

items.q: What are the Care Certificate 16 standards?
items.a: Skills for Care says there are now 16 standards, including one on awareness of learning disability and autism. Our guide to the standards goes through them. The CareStream course covers all 16.

items.q: Is there a free Care Certificate?
items.a: The CareStream course is CPD certified and free on every plan, in English on the Free plan. Translation is paid. It is a course that evidences completion, not the regulated qualification.

items.q: Can new carers do the Care Certificate online?
items.a: Yes, they can work through the course in the Staff Hub on their own phone. The practical side cannot be done online. Someone has to watch them work. See our guide to doing it online.

items.q: Where does the Care Certificate workbook fit in?
items.a: Your service may use a workbook as part of its own sign off. CareStream does not replace it. It is a CPD certified course and a record of your observation, and it does not replace workbook or assessor sign off.

items.q: How long does a new carer's induction take?
items.a: It varies by carer and by service. Our post on how long it takes explains the usual range and what affects it.

items.q: What is a Care Certificate observation?
items.a: It is when a competent person watches a new carer do the work and judges it. Skills for Care says workers are assessed on what they know and what they do. In CareStream you record the observation and a note, and the certificate then shows the sign off.

items.q: Who can be a Care Certificate assessor?
items.a: Skills for Care says the assessor needs a thorough understanding of, and direct experience in, what they are assessing. Your service chooses who. Read more in our post on choosing an assessor.

items.q: What does the CQC expect for new staff training?
items.a: Regulation 18 says staff must receive the support, training, professional development, supervision and appraisal they need for their duties. It does not list courses. See CQC and compliance for how the evidence builds up.

guide.heading: A practical way to run a new carer's observation
guide.lede: A course tells you what a carer knows. The observation tells you how they work. It does not need to be complicated, but it does need to be planned.

sections.h3: Plan it before the course ends
paragraphs: Book the observation in week two, not after the last quiz. Choose a task the carer does often, such as helping a resident to stand or giving personal care with dignity. Tell the carer what you will watch, so it feels like support and not a trap. Skills for Care describes assessment as covering both knowledge and practice, so it helps to treat the observation as half of the job.

sections.h3: Four checks for a good observation
checklist: Choose a competent colleague who knows the standard being assessed.
Watch a real task with a real resident, with their consent.
Write a short note straight away: what you saw, what went well, what to work on.
If something needs more practice, allocate a short adhoc module on that point and watch again.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the course results, any follow up lessons and your dated observation note together, so you can show that a carer was watched as well as tested.
